course.title: TypeScript: Static Typing for JavaScript
course.description: Add static types to your JavaScript - interfaces, generics, type-safe DOM code and Node.js projects.

lessons.title: Why TypeScript?
lessons.body:
Why TypeScript?

JavaScript is flexible, but that flexibility has a cost: a typo in a variable name or a wrong argument type only shows up when the code runs, often in front of a user. TypeScript is a typed superset of JavaScript — you write JavaScript plus optional type annotations, and the TypeScript compiler (tsc) checks your code and compiles it down to plain JavaScript that any browser or Node.js can run.

The compiler catches mistakes before the code runs: pass a string where a number is expected and you get a clear error at compile time, not a silent bug at runtime. Types also make the editor smarter — autocomplete, safe renaming and jump-to-definition all work because the editor knows the shape of your data. And because TypeScript is a superset, any valid JavaScript file is already valid TypeScript, so you can adopt it file by file.

function add(a: number, b: number): number {
  return a + b;
}
console.log(add(2, 3)); // 5
// add('2', 3); // Compile error: Argument of type 'string' is not assignable to parameter of type 'number'.

Step by step: a: number and b: number declare that both parameters must be numbers, : number after the parentheses promises a number result, and the compiler rejects the commented-out call because '2' is a string.

  • Key points
  • TypeScript is a typed superset of JavaScript that compiles to plain JavaScript.
  • The compiler catches type mistakes before the code runs.
  • Any valid JavaScript is valid TypeScript, so adoption can be gradual.
  • Types power editor autocomplete, safe renaming and refactoring.

mcqs.q: What is TypeScript?
options: A replacement for JavaScript that browsers run directly
A typed superset of JavaScript that compiles to plain JavaScript
mcqs.why: TypeScript adds optional static types to JavaScript and the tsc compiler turns it into plain JavaScript that browsers and Node.js can run.

mcqs.q: What does the TypeScript compiler (tsc) produce?
mcqs.why: tsc strips the type annotations and emits plain JavaScript files — browsers never run TypeScript directly.

mcqs.q: Which mistake does TypeScript catch that plain JavaScript misses?
options: Passing a string to a function that expects a number, caught before the code runs
mcqs.why: Static types let the compiler check argument types at compile time, so a type mismatch is an error before anything runs.

mcqs.q: Can valid JavaScript code run as TypeScript?
options: No, every file must be rewritten first
Yes — plain JavaScript is valid TypeScript
mcqs.why: TypeScript is a superset of JavaScript, so every JavaScript program is already a valid TypeScript program.

mcqs.q: What is the main benefit of static types in a large codebase?
options: The code runs faster in the browser
Errors are caught at compile time and editors can autocomplete and refactor safely
It removes the need for tests
It makes the JavaScript bundle smaller automatically
mcqs.why: Early error detection plus editor support (autocomplete, safe rename, jump to definition) is what pays off as a codebase grows.

tasks.title: Predict the output
tasks.answer: greet returns the string 'Hello, ' joined with 'Sid', so console.log prints Hello, Sid.
tasks.hint: What string does greet return when name is 'Sid'?

lessons.title: Types & Interfaces
lessons.body:
Types & Interfaces

Every value in TypeScript has a type. The primitives are string, number and boolean; arrays are written number[] or string[]. You declare a variable's type with a colon: let age: number = 19;. If you then assign a string to age, the compiler reports an error instead of letting the bug reach runtime.

Objects get their shape from an interface: a list of property names and their types. A ? after a property name makes it optional, so it may be left out. Interfaces are the way you tell TypeScript — and every other developer — exactly what an object must look like, and the compiler checks every object literal against them.

interface User {
  id: number;
  name: string;
  email?: string;
}
const user: User = { id: 1, name: 'Sid' };
const scores: number[] = [90, 85, 92];
// user.email is string | undefined because email is optional.

Step by step: the interface says a User has a number id, a string name and an optional string email; the object literal is checked against it and passes because only the optional property is missing; scores is checked as an array of numbers.

  • Key points
  • Primitive types: string, number, boolean; arrays: number[], string[].
  • An interface describes the shape of an object: property names and their types.
  • A ? after a property name makes it optional.
  • Assigning a value of the wrong type is a compile-time error.

mcqs.q: Which annotation declares a variable that holds text?
mcqs.why: string is TypeScript's type for text; text, str and char are not built-in types.

mcqs.q: What does the ? mean in `email?: string` inside an interface?
options: The property must be a number
The property is optional and may be omitted
mcqs.why: A ? marks an optional property: objects of that type may leave it out, and reading it gives string | undefined.

mcqs.q: What is an interface used for?
options: To describe the shape (property names and types) of an object
mcqs.why: An interface is a contract for an object's shape; the compiler checks every value against it.

mcqs.q: What type is `const scores: number[]`?
mcqs.why: The [] after a type means an array of that type, so number[] is an array whose elements are all numbers.

mcqs.q: What happens if you assign a string to a variable declared as number?
options: The TypeScript compiler reports a type error
mcqs.why: The declared type is a compile-time contract; assigning a string where a number is declared is a type error.

tasks.title: Fix the bug
tasks.prompt: This code does not compile. Fix it so the object matches the interface.
tasks.answer: The interface says id must be a number, but '1' is a string. Remove the quotes so id is the number 1.
tasks.hint: Check the type of each value against the interface — which one does not match?

lessons.title: Functions & Generics
lessons.body:
Functions & Generics

Functions in TypeScript carry types on both sides: each parameter gets a type and the return type goes after the parentheses — function add(a: number, b: number): number. A parameter with a default value, like b: number = 10, is optional and falls back to 10 when no argument is passed. Arrow functions work the same way: const double = (n: number): number => n * 2;.

Generics let one function work with many types without losing type safety. A type parameter such as <T> is a placeholder: when the function is called, TypeScript fills in the real type and remembers it. identity<number>(42) returns a number, while identity('hello') infers T as string and returns a string — unlike any, which throws all type information away.

function identity<T>(value: T): T {
  return value;
}
const n = identity<number>(42); // n is number
const s = identity('hello');     // T is inferred as string
function add(a: number, b: number = 10): number {
  return a + b;
}
// add(5) is 15, add(5, 1) is 6

Step by step: <T> declares the placeholder, value: T uses it as the parameter type, : T promises the same type back, and the call sites fill T in — explicitly with <number> or by inference from the argument.

  • Key points
  • Parameter types and the return type are written on the function signature.
  • A default value makes a parameter optional.
  • Generics use a placeholder type such as <T>, filled in at each call.
  • Generics keep the exact type; any discards it.

mcqs.q: What does `function add(a: number, b: number): number` declare?
options: A function taking two numbers and returning a number
A function taking two strings and returning a number
mcqs.why: The annotations say both parameters are numbers and the : number after the parentheses is the return type.

mcqs.q: What is a generic type parameter such as <T>?
options: A placeholder for a type, filled in when the function or type is used
mcqs.why: T stands in for a real type that is decided at each use, so one generic function can safely handle numbers, strings and objects.

mcqs.q: In `identity<number>(42)`, what is T?
mcqs.why: The <number> in the call explicitly fills in T as number, matching the argument 42.

mcqs.q: What does `b: number = 10` mean in a function signature?
options: b defaults to 10 if no argument is passed
mcqs.why: A default value makes the parameter optional: callers may omit it and 10 is used instead.

mcqs.q: Why use generics instead of `any` for a function like identity?
options: Generics keep the exact type through the function, while any throws type information away
any is not allowed in TypeScript
mcqs.why: With <T> the compiler knows identity(42) returns a number; with any it knows nothing about the result.

tasks.title: Fill in the blank
tasks.prompt: Fill in the missing type so this generic function accepts an array of T and returns its first element.
tasks.answer: items must be an array of T, written T[], so items[0] is a T (or undefined when the array is empty).
tasks.hint: items must be an array of T — how do you write an array type?

lessons.title: Type-Safe DOM Handling
lessons.body:
Type-Safe DOM Handling

The DOM is untyped by nature: document.querySelector('#email') returns Element | null because the element might not exist, and a plain Element has no value property. To read an input's value you assert the specific element type — as HTMLInputElement — which tells the compiler to treat the result as an input element.

Because the result can still be null, always guard before using it: an if (input) check or optional chaining ?. keeps a missing element from crashing the page. Event listeners are typed too — a 'click' handler receives a MouseEvent, so properties like clientX are checked by the compiler.

const input = document.querySelector('#email') as HTMLInputElement;
if (input) {
  console.log(input.value);
}
const btn = document.getElementById('save');
btn?.addEventListener('click', (e: MouseEvent) => {
  console.log('saved at', e.clientX);
});

Step by step: querySelector may return null, the assertion narrows it to an input element with a value property, the if guard handles the null case, and ?. skips the listener entirely when the button is missing.

  • Key points
  • querySelector returns Element | null — narrow it with as HTMLInputElement (or the matching element type).
  • Always guard against null before using a DOM element.
  • Optional chaining ?. skips a call when the value is null.
  • Event handlers receive typed events such as MouseEvent.

mcqs.q: Why does `document.querySelector('#email')` need a type assertion before you read `.value`?
options: It returns Element | null, and a plain Element has no value property — assert it as HTMLInputElement
mcqs.why: querySelector's return type is the generic Element, which has no value property; asserting HTMLInputElement gives access to it.

mcqs.q: What does `as HTMLInputElement` do?
options: It tells the compiler to treat the value as an HTMLInputElement
It creates a new input element on the page
It converts the element to a string
mcqs.why: A type assertion is a compile-time instruction: it narrows the value's type without changing the value at runtime.

mcqs.q: What does `btn?.addEventListener(...)` do if btn is null?
options: It safely skips the call — nothing happens
mcqs.why: Optional chaining ?. short-circuits on null or undefined, so the method is simply not called.

mcqs.q: What type is the event object in a 'click' handler?
mcqs.why: Click events are mouse events, so TypeScript types the handler's event parameter as MouseEvent.

mcqs.q: Why check `if (input)` before using `input.value`?
options: It makes the code run faster
querySelector can return null when the element is missing, and reading .value of null would crash
mcqs.why: A null guard handles the case where the selector matches nothing, which is exactly why the return type includes null.

tasks.title: Trace the code
tasks.prompt: Trace this code step by step. The page contains an h1 with id 'title'. What happens?
tasks.expected: el is the h1 element (not null), so the if branch runs and textContent becomes 'Welcome'; 'missing' is never logged.
tasks.answer: querySelector finds the h1, so el is not null; the if branch runs and sets the heading text to 'Welcome', and the else branch with console.log('missing') is skipped.
tasks.hint: Is el null when #title exists on the page?

lessons.title: TypeScript with Node.js
lessons.body:
TypeScript with Node.js

Node.js runs JavaScript, not TypeScript, so a TypeScript project is compiled first and the JavaScript output is run. Install the compiler with npm install -D typescript, create a tsconfig.json with npx tsc --init, and run npx tsc to compile every .ts file in src into JavaScript in dist.

The tsconfig.json controls the build: outDir is where compiled files go, rootDir is where source lives, target picks the JavaScript version to emit, and strict: true turns on the full set of type checks, including no implicit any. Node.js built-ins such as fs need their own type definitions, installed with npm install -D @types/node. Then you run the result with plain node dist/index.js.

// tsconfig.json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2020",
    "module": "commonjs",
    "outDir": "dist",
    "rootDir": "src",
    "strict": true
  }
}
import * as fs from 'fs';
const data: string = fs.readFileSync('notes.txt', 'utf-8');
console.log(data.length);

Step by step: tsc reads tsconfig.json, compiles src/index.ts to dist/index.js, the @types/node package supplies the types for fs, and node runs the compiled JavaScript.

  • Key points
  • Node.js runs the compiled JavaScript output, not the .ts files.
  • tsconfig.json sets outDir, rootDir, target and strict mode.
  • Install @types/node so TypeScript knows Node.js built-in APIs.
  • Compile with npx tsc, then run with node dist/index.js.

mcqs.q: What does `npx tsc` do?
options: It compiles TypeScript files into JavaScript
mcqs.why: tsc is the TypeScript compiler: it type-checks .ts files and emits equivalent .js files.

mcqs.q: What is tsconfig.json for?
options: It stores the compiler settings for the project
It lists the npm packages to install
It is the compiled JavaScript output
mcqs.why: tsconfig.json tells tsc how to compile the project — target, module system, output directory and strictness.

mcqs.q: Why install `@types/node` in a TypeScript Node.js project?
options: To give TypeScript type definitions for Node.js APIs such as fs and path
mcqs.why: Node.js ships no TypeScript types of its own; @types/node provides them so fs, path and friends type-check.

mcqs.q: What does `"strict": true` enable in tsconfig.json?
options: It makes the code run in the browser
It turns on strict type checking, including no implicit any
mcqs.why: strict mode enables the full family of strictness flags, catching implicit anys, possible nulls and more.

mcqs.q: After compiling a TypeScript Node.js project, how do you run it?
options: Run the .ts file directly with node
node dist/index.js on the compiled JavaScript output
mcqs.why: Node.js cannot run .ts files; you run the JavaScript tsc emitted, e.g. node dist/index.js.

tasks.title: Predict the output
tasks.prompt: What does this print on Linux?
tasks.answer: path.join joins the segments with the platform separator, which is / on Linux, so the result is src/app.ts.
tasks.hint: What separator does path.join use on Linux?

lessons.title: Project: Typed Task Manager
lessons.body:
Project: Typed Task Manager

Time to put the whole course together: a task manager where every piece of data is typed. Start with a Task interface — an id, a title and a done flag — so a task can never accidentally be missing a field. Then build a TaskManager class that keeps a private array of tasks and exposes typed methods: add(title: string): void, complete(id: number): void and list(): Task[].

The compiler now guards the whole program: you cannot add a task without a title, mark a non-existent task done without the compiler noticing the wrong type, or return the wrong shape from list(). A small script at the bottom adds three tasks, completes one and prints the list — compile it with npx tsc, fix any errors the compiler reports, and run the result with Node.js.

interface Task {
  id: number;
  title: string;
  done: boolean;
}
class TaskManager {
  private tasks: Task[] = [];
  add(title: string): void {
    this.tasks.push({ id: this.tasks.length + 1, title, done: false });
  }
  complete(id: number): void {
    const task = this.tasks.find((t) => t.id === id);
    if (task) {
      task.done = true;
    }
  }
  list(): Task[] {
    return this.tasks;
  }
}
const manager = new TaskManager();
manager.add('Learn TypeScript');
console.log(manager.list());

Step by step: the interface fixes the shape of a task, the class stores tasks privately, add builds a valid Task object, complete finds the task by id and flips its flag, and list returns the typed array.

  • Key points
  • Model the data first with an interface, then build the class around it.
  • Private fields keep the task list safe from outside code.
  • Typed methods make wrong calls a compile-time error.
  • Compile with tsc and run the JavaScript output with Node.js.

mcqs.q: Why define a Task interface before building the manager?
options: It makes the page load faster
So every task has the same known shape — id, title and done — checked by the compiler
mcqs.why: The interface is the single source of truth for what a task looks like; every method and object literal is checked against it.

mcqs.q: What does `private tasks: Task[]` mean?
options: tasks is a single Task object
tasks is an array of Task objects, only accessible inside the class
tasks is shared between all classes
mcqs.why: Task[] is an array of Task, and private restricts access to code inside the TaskManager class.

mcqs.q: Which method adds a task to the manager?
mcqs.why: add takes a title, builds a Task object with done: false and pushes it onto the tasks array.

mcqs.q: What does `list(): Task[]` promise to its caller?
options: It returns an array of Task objects
mcqs.why: The return type Task[] says the method returns an array whose elements are all Task objects.

mcqs.q: What is the final step before running this project?
options: Compile with tsc, then run the JavaScript output with node
Open the .ts file in a browser
Rename the files to .js by hand
mcqs.why: Node.js runs JavaScript, so tsc must compile the TypeScript first and node runs the emitted output.

tasks.title: Build the Typed Task Manager
tasks.prompt: Build the Typed Task Manager: define a Task interface, a TaskManager class with add, complete and list methods, and a small script that adds 3 tasks, completes 1, and prints the list. Compile with tsc and run it with Node.js.
tasks.expected: A compiled program that prints 3 tasks with exactly 1 marked done; tsc reports no errors.
tasks.answer: Define the Task interface first, implement the class methods with typed parameters and returns, then compile and run — fix any type errors tsc reports before running.
tasks.hint: Start from the Task interface in this lesson and add one method at a time.
